HISTORY & PHYSICAL (SUPER DETAILED)

Consult Summary:
32-year-old man with 3-day history of watery diarrhoea (4–5×/day) with mild abdominal pain, single emesis, and possible low-grade fever; no blood/mucus, no clear dietary or travel trigger; clinically well-hydrated—most consistent with self-limited acute viral gastroenteritis.

History:
• Presenting complaint: “Bad diarrhoea” for 3 days.  
• Timeline/progression: Began suddenly; frequency and character unchanged over the 3-day period.  
• Frequency/character: 4–5 bowel movements per day, loose to watery; variable consistency throughout day.  
• Associated symptoms: Mild lower abdominal pain, one episode of vomiting, subjective low-grade fever, ↓ appetite.  
• Denies: Blood or mucus in stool.  
• Hydration/nutrition: Drinking fluids well; slight appetite reduction; no signs of dehydration per clinician observation.  
• Triggers/relievers: No recent travel, no suspicious food (“nothing dodgy”); no medications taken yet for diarrhoea or pain.  
• Review of systems (pertinent):  
  – Constitutional: Possible mild fever, no weight loss reported.  
  – GI: As above; denies hematochezia, melena.  
  – Respiratory, GU, derm, neuro: Not discussed.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma – longstanding; currently uses inhaler “Lexapro” (name uncertain). Complications not discussed.

Social History:
• Residence: 231 Leonard Street, London (confirmed).  
• Occupation, exercise, diet baseline, finances: not discussed.  
• Smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs: not discussed.

Family History:
• Father: Hypertension; died of bowel cancer at age 62.  
• No other family history recorded.

Physical Examination:
(Vitals not recorded.)  
General: Clinician observes patient appears well and “not dehydrated.”  
No additional exam findings documented.

Investigations:
• None ordered or available at this visit.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Acute watery diarrhoea, likely infectious (probable viral gastroenteritis):
  • Assessment: Fits typical 3-day self-limited course with low-grade systemic features; no red-flag features (blood, severe pain, high fever, travel).  
  • Plan:  
    – Hydration: Encourage liberal oral fluids.  
    – Oral rehydration salts: Recommend OTC Dioralyte.  
    – Diet: “Soft” bland diet—crackers, toast, jam, mashed/boiled vegetables; avoid dairy (except yoghurt), eggs, fish, meat for ≥48 h after last loose stool.  
    – Probiotics: Yoghurt allowed to restore gut flora.  
    – Education: Warning signs—frequency ≥6–8 stools/day, dehydration features, blood in stool, persistence >1 week—seek medical review; may require stool culture and antibiotics if blood present.  
    – Follow-up: Re-contact service or seek urgent care if above red flags occur.

Issue 2 – Asthma:
  • Stable; using inhaler “Lexapro” (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
  • Plan: No changes today; verify correct inhaler and technique at next review.

Issue 3 – Family history of colorectal cancer:
  • Patient’s father died at 62; no current red-flag bowel symptoms.  
  • Plan: Document family history; routine age-appropriate colorectal screening when due; advise earlier evaluation if chronic bowel changes, blood in stool, or weight loss develop.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Acute viral gastroenteritis – High likelihood: Short, self-limited watery diarrhoea with mild vomiting/fever, no blood, no travel trigger.  
2. Acute bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis – Moderate likelihood: Similar presentation; less likely as no high-risk meal/travel and no blood/high fever.  
3. Medication-induced diarrhoea (if “Lexapro” = escitalopram) – Low-moderate likelihood: Possible SSRI side-effect, but unclear that patient takes SSRI and onset seems acute after chronic use.

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing expected elements: Comprehensive vitals, full physical exam, complete medication list with doses/frequencies, allergy confirmation (documented as none), smoking/alcohol history.  
• Conflicts: Name “Lexapro” given as inhaler—conflicts with usual SSRI formulation (conflict noted).  
• Transcript quality: Clear; occasional mishearing of medication name.
